steps.intro: Feedback is a short written note from one person about another's work. This walkthrough only looks around — nothing is saved, and you can replay it any time from the "How feedback works" button.
steps.lifecycle: A feedback starts as Requested (someone asked for it) or as your own Draft, and reaches people only when it is Sent. A request can be Rejected, and a sent feedback can be Withdrawn.
steps.received: Received lists feedback others sent you. You never see a draft — only what has been sent.
steps.provided: Provided is everything you write: drafts, sent feedback, and requests waiting for you (status Requested). Open a request to pick it up or decline it.
steps.team: My team shows feedback about the people who report to you — only once it is sent. Drafts stay private to their author.
steps.teamScope: Under Filters, "Reports" switches between your direct reports and everyone below you. The other filters narrow by person, status and visibility.
steps.new: Writing feedback starts here. Let's open the form to look — nothing is saved until you press a save button.
steps.setup: Pick up to four recipients, then choose who may read it: Provider + subject keeps it between you, Public shows it on the Kudos wall.
steps.actions: Save draft keeps it private until you are ready; Save & send delivers it. You can still withdraw a sent feedback later.
steps.ask: Want feedback about yourself? On a person's card use "Ask for feedback" — they get a request in their Provided tab.
steps.request: As a manager you can also use "Request feedback for" on a report's card to ask someone else about them. You see that it exists, and read it once the provider sends it.
steps.kudos: Public, sent feedback appears on the Kudos wall for everyone. That's the whole flow — Done takes you back to Feedback.

steps.intro: A goal is something your manager sets for you and tracks over time. This walkthrough only looks around — nothing is saved, and you can replay it any time from the "How goals work" button.
steps.lifecycle: A goal starts as a Draft, goes live as Active, and ends as Archived with a summary. Every step can be reversed — an active goal can return to draft, and an archived one can be reopened.
steps.own: My goals lists every goal your managers set for you, drafts included. You see a goal from the moment it is created, not only once it is active.
steps.filters: Under Filters you narrow the list by title, status and creation date. The choice is remembered the next time you come back.
steps.progress: While a goal is Active, both you and your manager record progress: tick milestones on a Plan, or enter the current value on a Number or Percentage goal. An optional comment lands in the goal's history, and the other side is notified.
steps.managed: Goals I've set lists the goals you set for your reports. Under Filters, "Reports" widens it from your direct reports to everyone below you.
steps.new: Creating a goal starts here. Let's open the form to look — nothing is created until you press Create.
steps.definition: Pick the team member, give the goal a title, choose its kind — Plan with milestones, Number or Percentage with a target — and set a due date. A new goal always lands as a Draft.
steps.actions: Create saves the draft and then asks whether to activate it right away. We won't press it now — nothing is created in this walkthrough.
steps.manage: On a goal's page you run its lifecycle: Activate a draft, Return to draft an active goal, Archive it with a summary, or Reopen an archived one. Only the manager who set the goal can do this.
steps.subordinates: Each card on My subordinates has a Goals button listing what you set for that person, and New goal to add one. The card also counts their active goals.
steps.managers: Each card on My managers has a Goals button showing the goals that manager set for you, and counts the active ones. That's the whole flow — Done takes you back to Goals.

steps.intro: Days off are absences you record yourself — nobody approves them. Paid days come out of a yearly budget per pool and unpaid ones are unlimited; this walkthrough only looks around — nothing is saved, and you can replay it any time from the "How days off work" button.
steps.calendar: Calendar is the leave planner: one row per person on your teams, paid days in teal, unpaid in gray, half days half-filled. Weekend and public-holiday columns are shaded.
steps.scope: Whose calendar switches between your teams, your direct reports and all your reports, including indirect ones. On the reports scopes each person's team shows under their name.
steps.month: Flip months with the arrows — the calendar always opens on the current month. Hover a shaded column header to see which public holiday it is.
steps.requests: My days off lists every entry of yours, newest first. There is nothing to approve or cancel — Delete is the only action, and a deleted entry frees its days at once.
steps.budget: Your paid days off shows, per paid pool, the allowance, what you have used and what remains this year. Unused days carry over to next year or reset every January, depending on the pool kind.
steps.team: My team lists your reports' entries — direct reports by default, or your whole chain under "Reports". You can delete any of them, just as the owner can.
steps.teamView: Entries | Budgets switches to one row per report and pool, where you set the yearly allowance and add corrections. Both views follow the Reports scope.
steps.record: Record days off records an absence on a report's behalf — for example to backfill vacation history. It is the same form you use for yourself, plus a report picker.
steps.new: Recording your own days off starts here. Let's open the form to look — nothing is recorded until you press Submit.
steps.form: Pick Paid from one of your pools or Unpaid, then the first and last day — one entry stays within one calendar year, and either edge can be a half day. The preview below counts working days only: weekends and public holidays are free.
steps.actions: Submit records the entry at once — your teammates and your manager are notified, and you can delete it later from My days off. We won't press it now; Done takes you back to Days off.

steps.intro: A performance review is your manager's assessment of one review period — five categories, each rated 1 to 6 with a written summary. This walkthrough only looks around — nothing is saved, and you can replay it any time from the "How performance reviews work" button.
steps.lifecycle: A review starts as a Draft only its author can see, moves to Calibration where the managers above can compare it, and is Published to you at the end. Every step can be reversed — a published review can be unpublished, a calibration returned to draft — and a review never skips Calibration.
steps.own: My performance lists the reviews published about you, newest period first. You see a review only once it is Published — drafts and calibration stay with the managers — and a notification tells you when one arrives.
steps.filters: Under Filters you narrow the list by manager, period and status. The choice is remembered the next time you come back.
steps.categories: Every review rates five categories — Attitude, Delivery, Skills, Aptitude and Overall — from 1, doesn't meet expectations, to 6, exceptional, each with a written summary. A review's page shows them on its Content tab; History lists every change, and Lifecycle explains the stages.
steps.managed: Team's performance shows one row per report for the selected period: their review's status and ratings, or "No review yet". Only the review's author can edit it; from Calibration on, managers above the author can read it too.
steps.period: The Period picker scopes the whole tab — it opens on the latest period, and the one containing today is marked Current.
steps.views: Table | Distribution | Quadrants are three views of the same people: the completion table, rating-balance charts per category, and a two-axis plane that places everyone by two categories of your choice.
steps.dashboardFilters: Under Filters, "Reports" widens the scope from your direct reports to everyone below you, and Team plus the career filters narrow it. Sorting and paging work on the filtered rows.
steps.new: A report without a review for the period shows New review in their row — one review per person and period. Let's open the form to look — nothing is created until you press Create.
steps.form: Pick the team member and the period. Periods still in the future can't be chosen, and a report who already has a review for that period is refused with a link to the existing one.
steps.actions: Create saves an empty draft and opens the editor, where you rate the five categories and write the summaries. We won't press it now — nothing is created in this walkthrough.
steps.manage: On a review's page you run its lifecycle: Submit for calibration once all five ratings and summaries are filled, Return to draft, Publish, or Unpublish. Only the manager who wrote the review can do this, and the report is notified when it is published or unpublished.
steps.periods: Reviews attach to Review periods — a global timeline an administrator extends without gaps; a period can't be changed once added, and a review needs a period that has started. That's the whole flow — Done takes you back to Performance.

steps.intro: A 1:1 meeting is a dated record of what you and your manager discussed — points, decisions and action items — written by the manager after the meeting. This walkthrough only looks around — nothing is saved, and you can replay it any time from the "How 1:1 meetings work" button.
steps.own: I'm a subordinate lists every 1:1 your managers documented with you, newest first, with counts of points, decisions and action items — and how many are still open. Open one to read it: the manager writes, you read.
steps.filters: Under Filters you narrow the list by manager name and meeting date. The choice is remembered the next time you come back.
steps.document: A meeting's page has three lists — Points discussed, Decisions made and Action items. Each action item has an owner, you or the manager, an optional due date and an Open or Resolved state, plus a history icon that follows the item across meetings.
steps.carryOver: Action items still open when the next 1:1 is created are carried over into it automatically, marked "Carried over since" the meeting they first appeared in, until someone resolves them. Only the pair's latest meeting can be edited — older ones are the record.
steps.managed: I'm a manager lists the 1:1s you documented with your reports. The pair's latest meeting shows Edit; older ones open read-only.
steps.team: My subordinate's a manager shows the 1:1s your reports run as managers themselves — direct reports by default, or your whole chain under "Reports" in Filters. Read-only: a look at how your managers manage.
steps.new: A new 1:1 starts here, or from a report's card on My subordinates. Let's open the form to look — nothing is created until you press Create.
steps.form: Pick the team member — anyone below you, indirect reports included — and the meeting date. A meeting can't be dated before the pair's previous one, so meetings stay in order.
steps.actions: Create saves the meeting and opens the editor, where you write the points, decisions and action items — and the open items from the previous 1:1 are already waiting there. We won't press it now — nothing is created in this walkthrough.
steps.edit: In the editor you add and reorder paragraphs, assign each action item to you or the report with a due date, and tick items resolved. Save replaces the whole document and notifies the report; only the pair's latest meeting is editable, and deleting it makes the previous one editable again.
steps.subordinates: Each card on My subordinates shows the Last 1:1 with that person and how many action items are open, and its 1:1 meetings menu offers New 1:1 and the list of your meetings together.
steps.managers: Each card on My managers shows your Last 1:1 with that manager and the open action items, and its 1:1 meetings menu lists every meeting you had together. That's the whole flow — Done takes you back to 1:1 meetings.
